extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/aesthetics; those studying aesthetic theory and cultural education
extracted.subtask_short: aesthetic theory of beauty and culture
extracted.subtask_description: Develops evaluative principles for beauty, culture, and human perfection by analysing three impulses (sensuous, formal, play) and prescribing how art and education should balance them. Explains what counts as beauty (a 'living form') and how culture must temper competing impulses without suppressing either.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of taste attending only to form
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste only attends to the form and never to the substance; it ends by placing the soul on the dangerous incline, leading it to neglect all reality and to sacrifice truth and morality to an attractive envelope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: when aesthetic judgment privileges appearance over substance, it can divert talent from serious activity, encourage vices compatible with a graceful exterior, and erode truth and social virtue. Historical examples are invoked (decline of liberties accompanying flourishing art) to illustrate the social cost of a purely formal taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty must be grounded in a pure/rational idea, not mere experience
rubrics_metrics.description: This pure and rational idea of the beautiful…cannot be taken from any real and special case, and must, on the contrary, direct and give sanction to our judgment in each special case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: seek the idea of beauty by abstraction and transcendental deduction from the possibility of a nature both sensuous and rational. Do not rely solely on empirical appearances when defining the beautiful; test particular cases against the pure idea of humanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between person (permanent) and condition (changeable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstraction arrives at two primary ideas…That which continues it names his person; that which changes his position, his condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual criterion: in evaluating human actions or representations, maintain the ontological distinction that person (I) persists while conditions change. Ethical/aesthetic judgments must respect that personality cannot be founded on changing conditions and that conditions require a temporal foundation (time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensuous instinct (material impulse) as evaluative dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: The sensuous instinct…issues from the physical existence of man…and it is this instinct which tends to enclose him in the limits of time, and to make of him a material being. This instinct requires that there should be change, and that time should contain something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating art or culture, recognise the legitimate claim of sensuousness: receptivity, vivid sensation, breadth of experience. Its perfection is greatest mutability and extensiveness (maximising contact with the world). But it must be constrained so it does not swallow personality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal instinct (rational impulse) as evaluative dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal instinct…issues from the absolute existence of man, or from his rational nature, and tends to set free, and bring harmony into the diversity of its manifestations, and to maintain personality notwithstanding all the changes of state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative role: the formal impulse supplies laws, universality and necessity for judgments and actions (truth and duty). Its perfection is the greatest possible independence and intensity of the determining faculty. It must be guarded from becoming merely receptive or suppressing the sensuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture's task: give equal justice to sensuous and formal impulses
rubrics_metrics.description: The office of culture is to watch over them and to secure to each one its proper limits; therefore culture has to give equal justice to both, and to defend not only the rational impulsion against the sensuous, but also the latter against the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive: cultural education and aesthetic formation must both cultivate receptivity (to enlarge sensuous contact) and strengthen autonomy (to secure personality). Tempering must be an active, moral act (not mere blunting of senses or relaxation of thought).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instinct of play as the aesthetic synthesising criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The instinct of play…will have as its object to suppress time in time, to conciliate the state of transition or becoming with the absolute being, change with identity. The sensuous impulsion wishes to be determined… the formal impulsion wishes to determine itself… the instinct of play will endeavor to receive as it would itself have produced, and to produce as it aspires to receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic judgment: beauty arises where the sensuous and formal impulses cooperate—i.e., when a form is also alive and life is formed. Evaluate works by their capacity to reconcile change and permanence, desire and law, giving the impression that life and form are mutually realised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty defined as living form (union of life and form)
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of the play instinct…may therefore bear the name of living form; a term that serves to describe all aesthetic qualities of phenomena, and what people style, in the widest sense, beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for beauty: something is beautiful insofar as its form is alive and its life is formed—i.e., its sensuous content is governed by formal necessity and its form embodies real, living content. Examples: sculpted marble can become a living form by the artist; a living person can be beautiful only when life and form coincide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection requires maximal receptivity and maximal autonomy together
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the world is developed in time…the perfection of the faculty that places men in relation with the world will necessarily be the greatest possible mutability and extensiveness. Since personality is permanence in change, the perfection of this faculty…will be the greatest possible freedom of action (autonomy) and intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational criterion: aim to increase both sensitivity to the world (receptivity) and the independence/intensity of the determining faculty (autonomy); culture consists in expanding receptive contacts and strengthening the will/understanding so both operate together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inversion errors: do not let one impulse dominate
rubrics_metrics.description: Man can invert this relation, and thus fail in attaining his destination in two ways…If the sensuous impulsion becomes determining…he loses as object what he gains in force. If the formal impulsion becomes receptive…he loses as a subject and autonomous force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative criterion: artistic or moral failures occur when reception substitutes for determination or vice versa. Evaluate practices that let sensation legislate (loss of personality) or let abstract form replace living content (loss of reality) as defective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper impulses by active moral and aesthetic agency, not by impotence
rubrics_metrics.description: This tempering…ought not to be the effect of physical impotence or of a blunting of sensations…It must be a free act, an activity of the person, which by its moral intensity moderates the sensuous intensity…In its turn, the tempering of the formal impulsion must not result from moral impotence…It is necessary that the glorious source of this second tempering should be the fulness of sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive guidance for formation: restraint must come from strength—character moderates temperament; thought must be tempered by rich sensation rather than by weakness. In practice, cultivate moral intensity to shape sense and cultivate sensuous richness to humanise reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as enlargement, not frivolous limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: What you style limitation…I name enlargement. Consequently I should have said exactly the reverse: man is serious only with the agreeable, with the good, and with the perfect, but he plays with beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual corrective: do not dismiss beauty as mere frivolity or play; aesthetic play is the condition in which humanity is completed and enlarged. Evaluate art that appears 'playful' by whether it expands human capacities rather than merely distracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic ideals exemplified by cultures that cultivate play (Greek ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: We can immediately understand why the ideal form of a Venus, of a Juno, and of an Apollo, is to be sought…in Greece…if we contrast the Greek population…with the Roman people gloating over the agony of a gladiator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative criterion: look to cultural practices that integrate play, physical contest, and intellectual rivalry (Greek examples) as producing higher aesthetic ideals. Use cultural-historical exemplars to judge whether an artistic ideal truly realises the play-instinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason mandates the existence of beauty as completion of humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason is obliged to make this demand, because her nature impels her to completeness…and accordingly, as soon as reason issues the mandate, 'a humanity shall exist,' it proclaims at the same time the law, 'there shall be a beauty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical criterion: the claim that beauty must exist follows logically from the idea of humanity as requiring both sensuous and formal completeness. Use this transcendental standard to evaluate whether an aesthetic object contributes to human completion.
